newsitem.title: UK: Polish abortion law mirrors European trend.
newsitem.headline: Polish abortion law mirrors European trend.

text.p: Poland's move on Thursday to liberalise abortion brings its legislation into line with many other European countries, but there are vast contrasts on the continent in the way the law is applied.
In Roman Catholic Ireland, abortion remains illegal and many women travel to Britain for terminations.

In Russia, abortion, legal until the 12th week of pregnancy, remains the chief form of "contraception". Sheaths and other contraceptives are difficult to obtain outside the major cities and, where available, can be expensive or unreliable.
Consequently Russia had 2.58 million abortions in 1995 and 3.27 million in 1992. Attitudes were formed chiefly in Soviet times, when there was no church participation in any ethical argument.

The circumstances were markedly different in Poland, where the Roman Catholic church is strong and a Polish-born Pope has intervened in the debate, as well as in Catholic Belgium which did not legalise abortion until 1990.
The reigning Belgian King Bedouin briefly abdicated at the time in order not to have to sign the bill into law. Abortion is now possible up to 14 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion will now be available under Polish law, as in Russia, Hungary, Austria, Greece and Spain, until 12 weeks. In Britain it is legal up to 24 weeks, in Italy until 90 days on medical or socio-economic grounds.

Countries set varying conditions, stipulating often that a danger to the mother or serious hardship must be proven. Frequently these conditions are loosely applied, prompting anti-abortion campaigners to speak of "abortion on demand".
In Belgium, where 11,243 legal abortions were carried out in 1995, a woman must be proven to be "in distresss".

In Britain, two doctors must decide that a pregnancy constitutes a threat to the woman's physical or mental health or a risk to the physical or mental health of existing children in the family or that there is a risk of serious foetal abnormality.

In Germany, which recorded 103,000 abortions in 1994, a woman must go through a complex process in which counsellors are obliged to stress the embryo's "right to life" and look for ways to keep the baby. In the end, however, the woman decides the fate of the unborn child.
Anti-abortion lobbies are strong in many European countries but have nowhere approached the radicalism of the United States where armed attacks have been carried out on abortion clinics.
